newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, dollar rise, but bonds fall before Fed meeting.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, dollar rise, but bonds fall before Fed meeting.

text.p: Stocks and the dollar rose on Monday amid prospects the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates on Tuesday, but the bond market fell as it remained wary of inflation.
Coffee prices fell sharply on profit-taking from last week's run-up to 20-year highs.

The Dow Jones industrial average rose 34.21 points to 7,228.88, bouncing back from Friday's sell-off of nearly 140 points. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,390 to 1,056 on light volume of 345 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

With Wall Street investors reluctant to make big trades ahead of Tuesday's meeting of the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, activity was lighter than usual, which may have exaggerated the market's swings.

Economists are split nearly down the middle about the outcome of the Fed's deliberations, with a slight majority forecasting no change in monetary policy, according to a Reuters survey released Monday.

The inflation-fighting Fed raised short term interest rates by a quarter point at its last meeting in March but the gauges of inflation since then have shown some softening in the economy and few signs of price pressure.
Some analysts said the Fed's stated goal, that it could take 'pre-emptive' steps to fight against future inflation, would likely bring a raise in interest rates.
"It's a close call, but the Fed will probably tighten 25 basis points (one quarter percentage point)," said Frank McCormick, vice president and senior economist at Bank of America.
"The trend rate of GDP growth is about 4 percent, unemployment is down to 4.9 percent and there are some slight signs that core inflation is beginning to pick up," he said.
Traders were optimistic, however, that a modest rise in rates would not crimp stock prices.

Business was slow in bonds, with the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond off 5/32, which raised its yield to 6.92 percent from 6.91 percent at Friday's close. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.
In currency markets, the dollar rose to 1.7080 German marks late Monday from 1.6925 marks late Friday, but was nearly unchanged at 115.75 Japanese yen vs. 115.70 yen.
At the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for May delivery fell 21.25 cents to 255.25 cents in the last day of trading for the May contract.

It touched its life-of-contract high at 280 cents -- also the highest price since June 1977 -- in early trading before a wave of liquidation ahead of the noon expiry prompted a price collapse. July coffee ended down 6.90 cents at 246.25 cents.

Gold prices fell again as traders fretted about Germany's plan to revalue its central bank gold reserves and a possible interest rate rise this week by the Federal Reserve. June gold on the COMEX in New York ended $2.70 lower at $342.20 an ounce.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices fell sharply as traders took profits after a sharp rally on Friday which occurred despite evidence of rising oil supplies.
Crude oil for June delivery closed down 53 cents a barrel at $21.59, with June gasoline ending down 0.66 cent a gallon at 65.21 cents and June heating oil down 0.55 cent a gallon at 57.92 cents.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index closed 48.7 points lower at 4,645.2. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average added 165.02 points to 20,489.75.
